# The Research Compendium {#sec-compendium}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*The purpose of this article is to show how the R package
can be a suitable template for organizing files into a
research compendium to enhance the reproducibility of
research.*

[Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen]{.smallcaps}, *Packaging
Data Analytical Work Reproducibly Using R (and Friends)*
(2018)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at a
folder of scripts and spreadsheets and name what kind of
research object it is trying to be. You will also be able
to draw the line between what counts as raw input and what
counts as a derived product. Finally, you will be able to
say exactly which single build gate, `R CMD check`, a tidy
directory earns for free, and what that gate still leaves
unexamined.

## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 60 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder
vocabulary this chapter uses when it places a compendium
on it; no other chapter is assumed. Statistically, nothing
beyond reading a hazard ratio and a coefficient table, as
in the chapter's cohort and comorbidity examples, is
required. No R fluency beyond reading a short script and a
directory listing is assumed; this chapter writes almost
no code itself.

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to
answer:**

- Can you explain what a research compendium is, and
  trace its lineage from Gentleman and Temple Lang through
  `rrtools`?
- Can you justify why the R package is the compendium
  container, say precisely what `R CMD check` thereby
  checks, and say what it does not?
- Can you enumerate the [Five Pillars](glossary.qmd#gloss-the-five-pillars)
  of a compendium and
  name the single artifact that captures each?
- Can you distinguish the five compendium archetypes and
  state how their directory layout, their report, and
  their gates differ while the reproducibility machinery
  stays the same?
- Can you apply progressive disclosure to walk a project
  from one archetype to another without reorganizing it?

**Outline.**

- Where this sits on the stack: locatable, and nothing
  pinned yet.
- Orientation: a cohort analysis that is a scatter, not
  an object.
- The analyst's contribution: naming the archetype,
  fixing the raw-and-derived boundary, deciding what
  becomes a function.
- The compendium as the unit of reproducible work: where
  the idea comes from.
- The R package as the compendium container: `R CMD
  check` as a universal gate, and its limit.
- Building and maintaining the package skeleton: the
  `usethis` and `devtools` commands.
- The Five Pillars.
- The directory layout, concretely.
- The README and the data dictionary, including the
  README's computational requirements.
- The five archetypes, each with a health-sciences
  example.
- Progressive disclosure: one layout, several stages.
- Worked example: one compendium through two archetypes.
- The cohort, continued: this book's own compendium
  against the Five Pillars.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: from earlier chapters

A cohort analysis was tagged `v1.0-submission` in 2018
and pushed to a remote. In 2024 you check out that tag
and re-run it under the current R. The code matches the
tag, and it sets a seed before drawing bootstrap
resamples with `sample()`. Yet the bootstrap interval no
longer matches the paper. There is no lockfile and no
container. Drawing on @sec-crisis, @sec-levels, and
@sec-version-control, which determinant layer most likely
moved, which rung did the tag secure, and what would have
held that layer fixed?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

For the 2018 bootstrap interval that no longer matches,
the most likely layer is the R runtime. R 3.6.0, released
in 2019, changed the default sampler behind `sample()`,
so the same seed now draws different resamples, as
@sec-crisis shows. The tag is not at fault. It fixes the
analysis code and makes it locatable, which is L0 and no
more (@sec-version-control). The default RNG kind comes
with the R release, so it belongs to the runtime and is
fixed at L2 (@sec-levels). Because the rungs are
cumulative, L2 also needs a lockfile, which would rule
out package churn, the other candidate. An explicit
`RNGkind()` call in the analysis code would have fixed
the sampler as well.
:::
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

We begin by placing the chapter on the determinant stack
of @sec-levels. In the sense of pinning a package version
or a system library, this chapter captures nothing on
that stack. What it captures are the two layers that sit
above the packages and the system, the analysis code and
the input data, by making them locatable and organized in
the first place. @fig-stack-compendium marks these two
layers. A compendium is what first turns a scatter of files into
something a reader can find and name, and within which
the reader can locate the raw-versus-derived boundary.
This is the L0 rung and no further.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stack-compendium
#| fig-cap: 'The determinant stack of @sec-levels, with analysis code and input data marked as captured by this chapter. A research compendium does not pin a package version or an operating system; what it captures, for the first time, is that the code and the data are locatable, organized by convention, and separated into raw and derived, which is the L0 rung this chapter secures and the container the later chapters install L1 through L3 into.'
#| fig-alt: !expr determinant_stack_alt(captures = c('Analysis code', 'Input data'))
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = c('Analysis code', 'Input data'),
  title = 'The compendium captures locatability, not yet packages or environment')
```

## Orientation

Consider a first-year epidemiology student
who has spent three months on a cohort analysis. The
analysis is an incident-diabetes study drawn from a
registry, with a cleaning script, a handful of models,
four figures, and a draft of a results section. The work
exists, but it exists as a scatter. The cleaning script
sits in a downloads folder, and the models sit in a
second file that reads a spreadsheet whose path is
hard-coded to one laptop. The figures are loose `png`
files pasted by hand into a manuscript, and the record of
which package versions produced any of it is nowhere at
all. Nothing here is wrong as statistics. The difficulty
is that the analysis is not an object. It cannot be
handed to a colleague, cited, archived, or re-run,
because there is no single thing to hand over.

The remedy is to make the analysis one object. A
*research compendium* is that object. It is a single,
self-describing directory that bundles the code, the
data, the prose, and the record of the environment in
which the analysis was run. Its contents are organized by
convention, so that another person, or the same person a
year later, can find every part and regenerate the
result. The compendium is the third of the recurring
ideas of this book, after the levels ladder and the
capture-versus-validate distinction. It is also the one
that gives the other two something to act on. A
reproducibility level is a property *of* a compendium; a
validation gate is a check run *against* a compendium.

The compendium also sets the starting rung on the
ladder. Merely by being a version-controlled directory
whose parts can be located, a compendium reaches L0,
locatable. It is not yet L1, because nothing has pinned
the package versions. It is not yet L2, because nothing
has pinned the environment. And it is certainly not yet
L3, because nothing has re-run it and shown the numbers
to match a recorded baseline. The compendium provides the
container into which the later chapters install those
higher guarantees.

The remainder of the chapter proceeds as follows. The
three judgments that remain the analyst's alone come
first, and we then trace where the idea of the compendium
comes from and why the R package became its container. We
next set out the Five Pillars and the directory layout,
then the README, the data dictionary, and project-oriented
paths with `here`. The five archetypes follow, each with a
health-sciences example and a note of how it weighs the
chapters ahead. Lastly, we consider
progressive disclosure, work one compendium through two
archetypes, and measure this book's own compendium
against the Five Pillars.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the scatter is missing

The epidemiology student's three months of work already
contains correct statistics. What, precisely, does the
compendium add that the statistics alone do not supply?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The statistics already have correctness. What the
compendium adds is the property of being a single,
locatable object. That is, it is a thing that can be
handed to a colleague, cited, archived, and re-run. This
is possible because every part of it (the code, the data,
and eventually the environment record) lives in one
self-describing directory rather than scattered across a
laptop's folders and a manuscript's pasted figures.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Three judgments at the center of this chapter are the
analyst's alone. No tool scaffolds them. Getting them
wrong produces a tidy directory that is nonetheless the
wrong shape for the work.

1. **Naming the archetype.** The analyst must decide
   what kind of object the project is: a data analysis,
   a manuscript, a reusable package, a simulation study,
   or a blog. This choice governs the layout, whether a
   report is rendered, and which gates apply. It is a
   statement of intent, not a technical setting, and it
   is the organizing decision of the chapter.

2. **Fixing the raw-and-derived boundary.** The analyst
   must decide what is an immutable input and what is a
   product of the analysis. A file placed in
   `raw_data/` is a promise that it will never be
   modified; a file in `derived_data/` is a promise that
   it can always be regenerated from the raw inputs and
   the code. No program can draw this line, because it
   depends on where the analyst judges the science to
   begin.

3. **Deciding what becomes a function.** The analyst
   must decide which code is a throwaway pipeline step,
   belonging in `analysis/scripts/`, and which is a
   reusable procedure worth documenting and testing,
   belonging in `R/`. This judgment determines what
   `R CMD check` and the test suite will actually
   protect, and it is revisited continuously as a
   project matures.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: three judgments, one tool-free

A newcomer asks which of `zzcollab`'s commands tells the
analyst where the raw-and-derived boundary falls. What is
the honest answer?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

None of them. The framework's commands create the
directories (`raw_data/`, `derived_data/`) and enforce the
gates once the boundary is drawn. However, drawing the
boundary, like naming the archetype and deciding what
becomes a function, is a judgment about the science. It
is not a setting the tooling can infer from the files
themselves.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Research compendium.** A single self-describing
  directory bundling the code, data, prose, and
  environment record of an analysis, organized by
  convention so that it can be located and re-run.
- **R-package skin.** The minimal set of files
  (`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, an `R/` directory) that
  makes a directory a valid R package, and therefore
  checkable by the R build tools.
- **`R CMD check`.** The standard R command that builds
  a package, runs its tests, and applies dozens of
  standardized checks; here it is a universal
  integrity gate on the compendium's package skin
  (`R/`, the tests, `DESCRIPTION`). It does not check
  `analysis/`, which the build excludes.
- **The Five Pillars.** The five artifacts a compendium
  manages, one per capture point: the `Dockerfile`,
  `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, the source code, and the
  data.
- **Archetype.** The kind of research object a
  compendium is (data analysis, manuscript, package,
  simulation study, or blog), which varies the layout
  and the gates but not the underlying machinery.
- **Render gate.** A validation check that a report or
  document rebuilds cleanly from source; it applies to
  archetypes that carry a report and not to those that
  do not.
- **Raw versus derived data.** Immutable original
  inputs versus the processed datasets regenerated from
  them by code.
- **Progressive disclosure.** The property that one
  layout supports a project's evolution from one
  archetype to another with no reorganization.
:::

## The compendium as the unit of reproducible work

We turn now to the history of the idea, which is older
than its tooling and which explains the shape of the
modern object. Gentleman and Temple Lang, writing in
2007, proposed the compendium in its current sense: a
document that combines text, code, and data in a form a
reader can actually execute, rather than a paper that
merely describes an analysis performed elsewhere
[@gentleman2007]. The proposal drew on Knuth's earlier
notion of [literate programming](glossary.qmd#gloss-literate-programming),
in which prose and code
are woven into one source [@knuth1984]. For some years
the compendium remained an aspiration without a
conventional implementation. Peng, arguing that
reproducibility should be treated as a minimum standard
for computational science, sharpened the motivation
without settling the container [@peng2011].

The decisive move came from Marwick, Boettiger, and
Mullen. They observed that a container of exactly the
required shape already existed and was in daily use by
thousands of R developers: the R package [@marwick2018].
An R package, as standardized by Wickham [@wickham2015],
already provides a `DESCRIPTION` file recording metadata
and dependencies and an `R/` directory for reusable
functions. It also provides a `tests/` directory for unit
tests, a `vignettes/` directory for long-form prose, and
a rigorously specified build system. Marwick and
colleagues extended this layout with a single top-level
`analysis/` directory holding subdirectories for raw
data, derived data, scripts, figures, and the manuscript
itself. They packaged the whole as the `rrtools` tool.
The resulting compendium can be installed, tested, and
checked with the very same commands used for any R
package. Nust, Boettiger, and Marwick later wrote a
companion guide on how to *read* such a compendium. That
such a guide exists is a useful sign that the object had
matured enough to have a reading protocol at all
[@nust2018].

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why the R package, not a new format

Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen could have proposed a
wholly new compendium format instead of reusing the R
package. What did reusing an existing format buy that a
bespoke one would not have?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A build system, a validation tool, and tens of thousands
of developers already fluent in the convention, all for
free. A bespoke format would have needed its own checker
written from scratch and its own community taught to use
it. The R package, on the other hand, came with
`R CMD check` and a working ecosystem already attached.
:::
:::

## The R package as the compendium container

The choice of the R package as the container is the
most consequential design decision in this lineage. At
first it looks like a convenience, the reuse of a
familiar layout. However, it also makes an existing,
rigorous, and universal gate apply to the compendium's
package skin for free. In this section we state both
what that gate reaches and what it does not.

The gate is `R CMD check`. When R was designed as a
system for distributing statistical software, its
authors built a command that takes a package and
subjects it to dozens of standardized checks. The command
checks that the code parses and loads, that every
documented function matches its documentation, and that
declared dependencies are actually available. It also
checks that the examples run and that the tests pass. The
command was built to keep the tens of thousands of
packages on CRAN mutually consistent. By dressing a
compendium in the R-package skin, we inherit this entire
apparatus at no cost. A compendium that passes
`R CMD check` is one whose functions in `R/` load, whose
stated dependencies resolve, and whose tests succeed.
These properties hold in a clean process that carries
none of the author's accumulated and undeclared state.

The qualification 'in `R/`' is exact, not cautious. But
what, precisely, does the check examine? As
`rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck()` and `devtools::check()` run it,
`R CMD check` does not check the directory it is pointed
at. It checks the package tarball that `R CMD build` makes
from that directory, and the build omits every path
listed in `.Rbuildignore`. (Plain `R CMD check` on a
directory skips the build, but it parses R code only in
the package's own directories, such as `R/` and
`tests/`, so the scripts in `analysis/` go unparsed
either way.) A compendium lists `^analysis$`
there, as it must, because raw data, derived files, and a
manuscript do not belong in an installable package. The
consequence is that the check never sees `analysis/`. An
analysis script with a syntax error, or one that calls
`library()` on a package declared nowhere, passes
`R CMD check` with no error, warning, or note. The same
undeclared package used inside
a function in `R/` draws a WARNING ('`::` or `:::` import
not declared from'). The code in `analysis/` therefore
needs gates of its own. These are a render gate, which
executes it, and a dependency scan, which reads it for
packages that the lockfile does not pin. Both are
developed in @sec-verification.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

To see the claim hold: add a deliberate syntax error to
any script under `analysis/scripts/`, then run
`rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck('.')` (we ran this on a toy
compendium with R 4.6.1 and `rcmdcheck` 1.4.0) from the
project root. It reports zero errors, warnings, or notes,
because the broken file never entered the build. To make
the same claim fail on purpose, move the broken code, or a
function that calls an undeclared package, into a file
under `R/` instead, and run the check again. It now fails
or warns, because that file is part of what gets built.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A new compendium that omits `^analysis$` from
`.Rbuildignore`, or deletes the line while editing the
file by hand, does not fail silently. `R CMD build` then
tries to fold the raw data, the derived files, and the
rendered report into the installable tarball. This can
make the build slow or bloat the package beyond what CRAN
or a reviewer will tolerate. It can also fail outright on
a binary data file the build process cannot parse as
package data.
The fix is to treat `.Rbuildignore` as part of the
package skin, checked into version control like
`DESCRIPTION`, not as an incidental dotfile.
:::

The R-package structure is therefore part of what makes
a directory a compendium. Every archetype we shall meet
below, however different in outward shape, carries the
same minimal R-package skin. It follows that
`R CMD check` is the one gate that applies to all of
them. A manuscript compendium adds a render gate on top;
a simulation compendium adds a seeding discipline; a
package compendium leans on the check most heavily of
all; but the universal floor is the same. It is, however,
a floor under `R/` and the tests, not under the
analysis. This is one reason the analyst's third
judgment, what becomes a function, matters: code moved
into `R/` comes under the check, and code left in
`analysis/` does not. We return
to this point when we tabulate the archetypes, because it
is the thread that unifies them.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why an R package?

A colleague proposes to organize a compendium as a plain
folder with sensible subdirectory names, arguing that the
R-package files (`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`) are empty
ceremony for an analysis that is not a package anyone will
install. What is lost by this choice?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The plain folder can still be locatable and can still
hold all five artifacts, so it can in principle reach the
higher levels of the ladder. What is lost is the universal
gate. Without the R-package skin, `R CMD check` has
nothing to check, so there is no single, standard,
pre-built command that verifies the functions load, their
dependencies resolve, and the tests pass. Without the
skin, the analyst must then assemble an equivalent set of
checks by hand for every project. (The analysis scripts
are a separate matter; with or without the skin, they
need a render gate and a dependency scan.) The ceremony
is precisely the interface that makes an existing
verification apparatus apply.
:::
:::

## Building and maintaining the package skeleton {#sec-package-skeleton}

The R-package skin need not be written by hand. Two
packages automate it: `usethis` writes the files of the
skin, and `devtools` runs the development loop on top of
them. The chunk below lists the commands a compendium
needs, in the order a new project meets them.

```{r}
#| label: skeleton-tools
lock <- jsonlite::read_json('../../renv.lock')
lock_pkgs <- names(lock$Packages)
skeleton_tools <- c('usethis', 'devtools', 'pkgdown',
                    'pkgload', 'tinytest')
in_lock <- skeleton_tools %in% lock_pkgs
names(in_lock) <- skeleton_tools
in_lock
```

```{r}
#| label: skeleton-tools-text
#| include: false
code_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 0) {
    return('none')
  }
  x <- paste0('`', x, '`')
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(x)
  }
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ', '), 'and',
        x[length(x)])
}
skeleton_absent <- code_list(skeleton_tools[!in_lock])
skeleton_present <- code_list(skeleton_tools[in_lock])
desc <- read.dcf('../../DESCRIPTION')
desc_license <- desc[1, 'License']
desc_suggests <- trimws(desc[1, 'Suggests'])
```

```{r}
#| label: skeleton-commands
#| eval: false
# Not run here: several of these packages are outside
# renv.lock (see the text).
usethis::create_package('cohortstudy')
usethis::use_r('cohort')
usethis::use_cc0_license()
usethis::use_package('survival')
tinytest::setup_tinytest('.')
usethis::use_pkgdown()

devtools::load_all()
devtools::document()
devtools::check()
pkgdown::build_site()
```

We do not run the second chunk. Of the five tools it
calls, `r skeleton_absent` are not recorded in this
repository's `renv.lock`, so running them would step
outside the pinned library; only `r skeleton_present` are
recorded. That absence is defensible for development
tools, since what they produce (`DESCRIPTION`,
`NAMESPACE`, the help files in `man/`) is committed. A
reproducer uses those files without rerunning the tools,
and can run `R CMD check` from the shell with none of
them installed.

The first six calls run once, or once per new file.
`create_package()` writes `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, and
`R/`, the minimal skin of the previous section. `use_r()`
creates or opens a file in `R/`, the place where a
function comes under the check. The license call writes
the `License` field and a license file. This compendium's
`DESCRIPTION` records `r desc_license`. The call that
writes `CC0` is `use_cc0_license()`, and the choice of
license is argued in @sec-archiving. `use_package()` adds a package
to `Imports`, which is how the undeclared-import WARNING
of the previous section is cleared. Because the book tests
with `tinytest` [@vanderloo2020], its `setup_tinytest()`
takes the place of the `use_testthat()` most tutorials
show. It creates `inst/tinytest/` and the runner
`tests/tinytest.R`, and adds `tinytest` to `Suggests`,
where this compendium's `DESCRIPTION` has
`r desc_suggests`.

The next three calls form the loop that is repeated while
the code in `R/` changes. `load_all()` makes the
package's functions available in the session by
simulating a build, an install, and an attach, and
@wickham2023 recommend it over `source()` for package
work. It is supplied by `pkgload`, which this chapter's
own first chunk calls directly. `document()` turns the
roxygen comments above each function into help files and
regenerates `NAMESPACE`. `check()` builds the tarball and
runs `R CMD check` on it, the gate of the previous
section, with the same blind spot for `analysis/`. A
useful habit is to run `check()` before any commit that
touches `R/`, `DESCRIPTION`, or the tests.

`pkgdown` builds a website from the help files, the
README, and any vignettes. `use_pkgdown()` runs once and
writes `_pkgdown.yml`; `build_site()` is rerun to refresh
the site. A site is documentation, not a gate. It earns
its place in the R-package archetype, whose users read
reference pages, and is seldom worth maintaining for a
data analysis. The full treatment of each step, and of
the many `usethis` helpers not shown, is *R Packages*
(2e) by Wickham and Bryan [@wickham2023]. Its chapter 'The
Whole Game' runs the loop end to end on a toy package,
its 'Website' chapter covers `pkgdown`, and an appendix
treats `R CMD check` in detail.

## The Five Pillars

Having settled the container, we turn to what it holds.
A compendium is defined by convention, but it *manages* a
specific and small set of artifacts. The `zzcollab`
framework organizes these as the Five Pillars. These are
the five things a compendium reads, writes, and
version-controls, one for each point at which
reproducibility can be captured [@thomas2026zzcollab]. An
analysis is reproducible only to the extent that all five
are captured. Moreover, the pillars are layered rather
than independent, each resting on the ones beneath it.

1. **Computational environment**, captured by the
   `Dockerfile`. This pillar fixes the operating system,
   the R version itself, the system libraries, and the
   document toolchain, all the software beneath the R
   packages. It is the subject of @sec-containers.

2. **Package versions**, captured by `renv.lock`. This
   pillar records the exact version of every R package the
   analysis loads, so that the same set can be restored on
   another machine. It is the subject
   of @sec-dependencies.

3. **Session configuration**, captured by the project
   `.Rprofile`. This pillar fixes the R options, the
   locale and timezone, and the thread counts that shape
   a session before any user code runs. A profile can
   also override the random-number-generator kind, but
   such an override is secured only by an explicit
   `RNGkind()` call in the analysis code, and the seed
   belongs there too (@sec-levels, @sec-testing).

4. **Source code**, captured by the version-control
   history. This pillar holds the scripts, the functions,
   the manuscript source, and the tests that implement the
   analysis.

5. **Data**, captured either by inclusion in the
   compendium, for small redistributable files, or by
   reference to an external repository with a resolvable
   identifier, for large or restricted data.

Two of the pillars are not coordinate with the other
three. Source code and data, pillars four and
five, are the inputs whose re-execution is the goal. The
environment, packages, and session, pillars one through
three, are the conditions under which that re-execution
occurs. This chapter is about the container that holds all
five and the shape that container takes. The individual
pillars are developed in the chapters named against them.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: layered, not independent

Why does the chapter say the pillars are 'layered rather
than independent,' and what would it mean to capture
pillar two, package versions, while leaving pillar one,
the computational environment, uncaptured?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A lockfile restored outside any pinned environment still
depends on whatever R version and system libraries the
host machine happens to supply. Consequently, pillar
two's guarantee, 'the same packages,' is only as strong as
pillar one's, 'the same environment,' lets it be.
Capturing packages without the environment is exactly
@sec-levels's L1 without L2. It is a real step, but one
whose benefit a different R release or a missing system
library can still erase.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice stops at naming and separating
the five artifacts. It leaves their actual capture, and the
rung that capture buys, to the chapters named against each
pillar above.
:::

## The directory layout, concretely

We now make the layout concrete. The following is the
top-level structure of a `zzcollab` compendium. The block
is illustrative and is not executed.

```
penguin-analysis/
├── DESCRIPTION           # package metadata and dependencies
├── NAMESPACE             # generated; exported functions
├── LICENSE
├── R/                    # reusable, documented functions
├── man/                  # generated function documentation
├── tests/                # tinytest runner
├── inst/tinytest/        # unit tests (test-*.R)
├── vignettes/            # long-form prose
├── analysis/
│   ├── data/
│   │   ├── raw_data/       # immutable inputs
│   │   ├── derived_data/   # regenerable script outputs
│   │   └── metadata/       # data dictionaries, provenance
│   ├── scripts/           # numbered pipeline steps
│   ├── report/            # report.Rmd / index.qmd manuscript
│   ├── figures/           # generated figures
│   └── tables/            # generated tables
├── Dockerfile            # Pillar 1: environment
├── renv.lock             # Pillar 2: package versions
├── .Rprofile             # Pillar 3: session configuration
├── Makefile              # workflow entry points
├── zzcollab.yaml         # configuration: base image, archetype
├── .zzcollab-state       # generated state record; never hand-edited
└── .github/workflows/    # continuous-integration definitions
```

Above the `analysis/` directory sits the standard
R-package machinery, and this is the skin that makes
`R CMD check` apply. Within `analysis/` sits the research
proper, in the Marwick convention. Its raw-and-derived
data separation is the analyst's second judgment made
physical. At the root sit the three environment
artifacts, one per pillar. Alongside them sit the
`Makefile` that provides the commands and the
`zzcollab.yaml` that records, among a small set of
parameters, the archetype. That last file is our bridge
to the centerpiece of the chapter. The archetype is a
first-class parameter recorded there, elicited at
creation time alongside the choice of base image.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: finding the boundary in the tree

Using the directory listing above, name the one line that
marks the boundary `R CMD check` actually respects, and
state which side of that line `renv.lock` falls on.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The boundary is the `analysis/` entry itself, the one path
`.Rbuildignore` excludes from the build. `renv.lock` sits
outside `analysis/`, at the project root, so it is not
excluded by that line. However, it is also not parsed by
`R CMD check`, which reads `DESCRIPTION` for declared
dependencies rather than the lockfile. The two artifacts
answer different questions about the same package skin.
:::
:::

## The README and the data dictionary

The directory listing above names a `README` nowhere, and
that absence is not an oversight to copy. A compendium that
captures all five pillars perfectly but ships without a
`README` still fails the first test a stranger applies to
it, because the stranger has no entry point. The NHS RAP
Community of Practice makes a README one of the criteria
of its baseline level, alongside open-source code, version
control, peer review of the code, and open publication.
A repository meets the README criterion only once it
'includes a README.md file (or equivalent) that clearly
details steps a user must follow to reproduce the code'
[@nhsrap2024]. A `README.md` at the
project root should state, in order, what the project is
for, how to reproduce it, and where the data dictionary
lives for anyone who needs the columns rather than the
narrative. The reproduction instructions name the `make`
target or `Rscript` command that runs the pipeline end to
end, and the archetype-specific gate from @sec-levels that
passing it claims.

The data dictionary is a second, separate document, usually
in `analysis/data/metadata/` or beside the extract it
describes. It answers a question the README should not try
to: what is each column, exactly. At minimum it gives, per
column, the name, its type, a one-line meaning, its units
where numeric, and its provenance. Provenance here means
whether the column was measured, derived, or simulated and
by what script. This book's own `analysis/data/README.md`
is a worked, if unusually candid, example. Because the
extract it describes is synthetic, the dictionary can also
say outright which rows are planted defects and why. A real
data use agreement would instead replace that disclosure
with an access-control statement. The columns table there
(`mrn`, `patient_name`, `hba1c`, and seven more, each with
a type and a one-line meaning) is the shape to imitate. On
the other hand, the provenance section above it, naming the
exact generator script and seed, is the part a real project
cannot write the same way. A real extract's provenance is
the originating system and the extraction date, not a
committed script.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: README versus data dictionary

A compendium's `README.md` says 'run `make all` to reproduce
every figure in the report' and nothing else about the data.
Is this README sufficient on its own, and what, if anything,
is still missing from the compendium?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The sentence satisfies the README criterion of the RAP
baseline, since it states the one command a user must run;
the baseline's other criteria are separate. What is
missing is not part of the README's job: a data dictionary
naming each column's type, meaning, units, and provenance.
A reproducer who can rerun the pipeline but cannot tell what
`hba1c` means or whether it was measured or simulated can
regenerate the numbers but cannot interpret them.
:::
:::

### The README's computational requirements {#sec-readme-requirements}

A README that names the command still leaves a
reproducer guessing what the command needs. The template
README of the Social Science Data Editors, written for
replication packages, gives this a section of its own,
'Computational requirements' [@vilhuber2022readme].
Adapted to an R compendium, that section asks for the
first four items below, and the template's 'List of
tables and programs' supplies the fifth.

- **Software and versions.** The R version and every
  package, each at the version the author used. In a
  compendium the lockfile carries the list, and the
  README names the R version, points to `renv.lock`, and
  names the image digest once there is one.
- **Randomness.** A fixed seed, not one taken from the
  clock, and a statement of where each seed is set, or a
  statement that no random numbers are drawn. The
  template warns that parallel work and the order in
  which programs run both need care.
- **Runtime.** The wall-clock time of a full run, in a
  coarse category such as under ten minutes, and any
  storage needed beyond the repository itself.
- **Hardware.** The operating system, processor, and
  memory of the machine on which that time was measured.
- **A map from outputs to code.** Every table and
  figure, by its number in the manuscript, beside the
  program (and, where useful, the line) that produces
  it.

```{r}
#| label: readme-requirements
#| include: false
lock_r_version <- lock$R$Version
key_pkgs <- c('survival', 'withr', 'tinytest')
key_versions <- vapply(key_pkgs, function(p) {
  lock$Packages[[p]]$Version
}, character(1))
gen_path <- '../scripts/simulate_cohort.R'
gen_lines <- readLines(gen_path)
seed_line <- grep('^set\\.seed\\(', gen_lines)[1]
seed_call <- trimws(gen_lines[seed_line])
boot_seed <- formals(bootstrap_cox_ci)$seed
boot_b <- formals(bootstrap_cox_ci)$B
raw_csv <- '../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
run_secs <- system.time({
  canonical <- run_canonical_analysis(raw_csv)
  boot <- bootstrap_cox_ci(clean_cohort(load_cohort(raw_csv)))
})[['elapsed']]
run_category <- if (run_secs < 600) {
  'under 10 min'
} else if (run_secs < 3600) {
  'under 1 hour'
} else {
  'over 1 hour'
}
output_map <- data.frame(
  output = c('Synthetic extract', 'Cox HR for BMI, 95% CI',
             'Bootstrap interval', 'Recorded baseline',
             'Baseline check (L3)'),
  code = c('analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R',
           'R/cohort.R: run_canonical_analysis()',
           'R/cohort.R: bootstrap_cox_ci()',
           'analysis/scripts/generate_baseline.R',
           'inst/tinytest/test-baseline-cohort.R')
)
map_files <- c('analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R', 'R/cohort.R',
               'analysis/scripts/generate_baseline.R',
               'inst/tinytest/test-baseline-cohort.R',
               'inst/baseline/cohort_baseline.rds')
stopifnot(all(file.exists(file.path('../..', map_files))),
          !is.na(seed_line))
root_readme <- file.exists('../../README.md')
readme_excerpt <- c(
  '## Computational requirements',
  '',
  paste0('- Software: R ', lock_r_version,
         ', packages as in renv.lock'),
  '  (restore with renv::restore()); key packages',
  paste0('  ', paste(key_pkgs, key_versions, collapse = ', '),
         '.'),
  paste0('- Randomness: ', basename(gen_path), ' calls'),
  paste0('  ', seed_call, ' once, at line ', seed_line, ';'),
  paste0('  bootstrap_cox_ci() sets seed ', boot_seed,
         ' (B = ', boot_b, ')'),
  '  with withr::with_seed(). Sampler kinds:',
  paste0('  ', paste(RNGkind(), collapse = ', '), '.'),
  paste0('- Runtime: ', format(round(run_secs, 1), nsmall = 1),
         ' s for the analysis and bootstrap'),
  paste0('  (', run_category, ').'),
  paste0('- Hardware: ', R.version$platform, ', ',
         parallel::detectCores(), ' logical cores.'),
  '',
  '| Output                 | Produced by |',
  '|------------------------|-------------|',
  paste0('| ', formatC(output_map$output, width = -22), ' | ',
         output_map$code, ' |')
)
```

This book's cohort compendium makes a compact example.
Its repository `r if (root_readme) 'has' else 'does not yet have'`
a `README.md` at the root, so the excerpt below is the
section such a file would carry. Every value in it,
from the R version to the seed's line number and the
runtime, is read from the repository or measured when
this chapter is rendered, which is the same rule the
README itself should follow.

```{r}
#| label: readme-excerpt
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat('```markdown', readme_excerpt, '```', sep = '\n')
```

Two points in the excerpt are easy to miss. The extract
and the bootstrap draw from separate seeds, and the
README says where each is set, because a reader who finds
only one may assume the other draws from the clock. The
runtime and hardware are those of the machine that last
rendered this chapter, not of the reader's; they tell a
reproducer whether a run is expected to take seconds or
days, not what their own run will take. The excerpt also
omits memory, which base R does not report in a portable
way; an author measures it and adds the figure by hand.

## Project-oriented paths: `here`, not `setwd()`

A script that opens with `setwd('/Users/jane/project')`
reproduces on exactly one machine: Jane's. The fix taught by
the `here` package is to mark the project root once, with a
file such as `.here` or the marker RStudio and Git already
leave behind. Every path is then built with `here::here()`,
which walks up from the working directory until it finds
that marker and returns paths relative to it from there on
[@bryan2024safepaths]. Consider a script that reads
`here::here('analysis', 'data', 'raw_data', 'cohort_raw.csv')`.
It resolves the same file whether R is launched from the
project root, from `analysis/report/`, or from a
continuous-integration runner that checks the repository
out to a different absolute path each time. This holds
because the path is computed from the marker rather than
typed as a string.

This book's own chapters, inspected directly, show why the
discipline matters even without `setwd()`. Several chapters
reach the cohort extract with `'../data/raw_data/...'`.
However, `08-testing-quality.qmd` reaches the same file
with `'../../analysis/data/raw_data/...'`, which climbs to
the project root and back down again. From
`analysis/report/` the two strings name one file by
different routes, and nothing but the author's care keeps
the two forms in agreement. Every one of these paths works
only because the author tracked, chunk by chunk, how many
`../` steps the renderer's working directory is from the
target file. By contrast,
`here::here('analysis', 'data', 'raw_data',
'cohort_raw.csv')` would resolve identically from any of
these chunks, because it does not depend on the renderer's
starting point at all. The relative-path convention is not
wrong, exactly. It is fragile in a way that is invisible
until a chunk is moved, copied into a different chapter, or
run from a different tool.

## The five archetypes

We come now to the centerpiece of the chapter. In this
section we make the point this book returns to in every
chapter: a research compendium need not be a manuscript.
Once we have seen the `analysis/report/` directory, it is
easy to assume that a compendium always exists to render a
paper. That is the common case, but it is one case among
five.

`zzcollab` treats the research archetype as a first-class
initialization parameter, orthogonal to the choice of
computational environment [@thomas2026zzcollab]. Where
the base image fixes the environment, the archetype
determines the starting scaffolding: the directory
emphasis, whether a primary report exists, and which
validation gates apply on top of the universal one. Five
archetypes are advertised. Because
every one of them carries the minimal R-package skin,
`R CMD check` remains the universal gate across all five.
The framework's own whitepaper stresses this point in its
account of the archetype axis. The reproducibility
machinery is identical; what varies is the shape of the
work and the gates it warrants. We take each in turn, with
a health-sciences example, and then tabulate the
differences.

### 1. Data analysis (a cohort study)

The first archetype is the exploratory and confirmatory
data analysis with no manuscript as its primary organizing
document. This is the closest to the original `rrtools`
use case, and it is the archetype of the epidemiology
student of our orientation. The work lives in
`analysis/scripts/`, as numbered pipeline steps, and in
`analysis/figures/`, with the derived datasets in
`analysis/data/derived_data/`. Consider an
incident-diabetes cohort study. A cleaning script reads
the registry extract from `raw_data/` and writes an
analysis-ready table to `derived_data/`. A modeling
script fits a Cox proportional-hazards model and writes
the coefficient table to `tables/`, and a plotting script
writes the Kaplan-Meier curves to `figures/`. There may be
a short results document, but the deliverable is the
pipeline and its outputs.

The applicable gates are the universal `R CMD check` and
the unit tests. The latter guard the cleaning logic and
the data invariants. For example, they check that the
cohort has the expected number of subjects. They also check that
a derived rate matches a value recorded in a baseline file
within a stated tolerance, rather than merely falling in a
plausible range. A render gate is optional here, because
there may be no report to render. The reproducibility
machinery, environment and packages and session, is
nonetheless present in full.

### 2. Scholarly manuscript (a comorbidity paper)

The second archetype makes the manuscript the organizing
principle. A `report.Rmd` or `index.qmd` file in
`analysis/report/` is created on day one and written in
parallel with the analysis, so that the prose and the
numbers never drift apart. Every figure in the paper is
regenerated on each render, rather than pasted in by hand. A
representative deployment is a study of the comorbidity of
PTSD, depression, and diabetes among Black women drawn from
a trauma-study cohort. The study uses variable selection,
multiple imputation, and causal mediation analysis. The
compendium
organizes the manuscript in `analysis/report/report.Rmd`,
the statistical functions in `R/` with `roxygen2`
documentation, the analysis pipeline in
`analysis/scripts/`, and the imputed datasets in
`analysis/data/derived_data/`.

Here the render gate is central, not optional. A
validation run rebuilds the report from source, and a
failure to render is a failure of the compendium. The gates
are therefore `R CMD check`, the unit tests, and the render
of `report.Rmd` to PDF. This is the archetype most readers
imagine when they hear the word compendium, and it is only
the second of five.

### 3. R package (a summary-table package)

The third archetype arises when the reusable code matures
into something of general interest. At that point `R/`,
`man/`, and `tests/` become the first-class content, and
the compendium is shareable as a CRAN-style package. What
distinguishes this archetype is that *there is no report
to render at all*. A package that generates
publication-quality clinical-trial summary tables has no
manuscript as its deliverable; its
deliverable is the exported, documented, tested function. A
representative deployment is exactly such a summary-table
package, hosting its source in `R/`, its examples in
`vignettes/`, and its
documentation as a generated website.

The gates for this archetype are `R CMD check`, run at its
full strength, and the unit tests. There is no render gate,
because there is nothing to render. This case is the
clearest refutation of the manuscript-only view. An
entirely valid, fully reproducible compendium can produce
no report whatsoever, and its integrity rests on the
universal check and the tests alone.

### 4. Simulation study (a power analysis)

The fourth archetype is the simulation study, such as a
power calculation or an assessment of the operating
characteristics of a proposed trial design. In such a
study the compendium enumerates a grid of parameter
configurations, runs Monte Carlo replicates at each, and
stores the results. The layout leans on
`analysis/scripts/` for the simulation driver and on
`analysis/data/derived_data/` for the stored replicate
results. These are treated as derived data because they
can be regenerated from the code and the seeds.

But what makes a simulation reproducible at all? The
distinguishing discipline of this archetype is *seeding*.
A simulation whose random draws are not pinned by an
explicit `set.seed()` is not reproducible even in
principle, because a second run produces different numbers
by construction. The archetype therefore emphasizes
explicit seeding and parallel execution. A recommended
practice is to store a seed column alongside the parameter
grid so that each replicate is individually reproducible.
Consider a power simulation for a longitudinal trial. The
driver builds a grid over sample size and effect size and
assigns each row an integer seed. It then simulates a
dataset for each row, fits the planned model, and records
whether the null was rejected. The empirical
power is then the rejection rate within each cell. The
gates are `R CMD check`, the unit tests, and, as an
emphasis particular to this archetype, a baseline test
that compares the seeded output with a value recorded in
an earlier session and committed (@sec-testing). A second
call in the same session is not such a test, because it
agrees with the first even when the generator has
changed. A render gate is optional, since the deliverable is
often the stored results rather than a paper.

### 5. Blog (a teaching notebook)

The fifth archetype is the blog or lab notebook, in which
the compendium renders, in the general case, not one report
but many documents. A teaching blog carrying a series of
methods posts, or a running lab notebook of analyses, is a
single compendium. Its `analysis/` tree may hold many
`index.qmd` files, each rendered to a static site by the
same machinery that renders a manuscript. The framework's
representative deployment is the limiting case of a single
post. Integration with Quarto [@allaire2024] enables
publication to the site from the same compendium that
produced the underlying analyses. As a result, the full
five-pillar reproducibility stack applies to web-published
teaching content without any change to the workflow.

The gate here is again the universal `R CMD check`, joined
by a render gate that must succeed for *each* post the
compendium carries. The multiplicity is the distinguishing
feature of the general case. That is, a blog compendium is
a render-many, where the manuscript is a render-one and the
package is a render-none.

The five archetypes and their differences are summarized
in @tbl-archetypes, and @fig-gates shows which validation
gates apply to each. Both are best read across the rows,
to see how the layout and the gates vary, and down the two
universal columns, to see how much stays fixed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-archetypes
#| tbl-cap: 'The five research-compendium archetypes. The reproducibility machinery is identical across all five; only the directory emphasis, the presence of a rendered report, and the gates that apply on top of the universal R CMD check differ.'

library(tibble)
library(knitr)

archetypes <- tibble::tibble(
  archetype = c(
    'Data analysis', 'Scholarly manuscript', 'R package',
    'Simulation study', 'Blog'
  ),
  directory = c(
    'analysis/scripts/, analysis/figures/',
    'analysis/report/',
    'R/, man/, tests/',
    'analysis/scripts/, derived_data/',
    'many analysis/ index.qmd posts'
  ),
  report = c(
    'Optional', 'Yes, to PDF', 'No',
    'Optional', 'Yes, many'
  ),
  gate = c(
    'R CMD check and tests',
    'R CMD check plus render',
    'R CMD check and unit tests',
    'R CMD check plus seed determinism',
    'R CMD check plus render of each post'
  ),
  example = c(
    'Incident-diabetes cohort analysis',
    'PTSD and diabetes comorbidity paper',
    'Clinical-trial summary-table package',
    'Power and operating-characteristics simulation',
    'Teaching blog or lab notebook'
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  archetypes,
  col.names = c(
    'Archetype', 'Directory emphasis', 'Renders a report?',
    'Primary validation gate', 'Health-sciences example'
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gates
#| fig-cap: 'Validation gates by archetype. The R-package check and the unit tests apply universally; the render and seeding gates apply selectively. Where a render gate is only optional, as for a data analysis or a simulation study without a report, the cell is left unmarked. The underlying reproducibility machinery, the Five Pillars, is identical across every row.'
#| fig-alt: 'A grid of five archetype rows (data analysis, scholarly manuscript, R package, simulation study, and blog) against four gate columns (R CMD check, unit tests, render report, and seed determinism). Universal cells use a dark blue fill with a white filled circle, selective cells a dark green fill with a white filled triangle, and cells where the gate does not apply are a medium blue-gray without a symbol. Every cell in the R CMD check and unit tests columns is universal, ten circles in all. The render report column is selective for scholarly manuscript and blog, and the seed determinism column is selective for simulation study only, three triangles in all. A legend below the grid keys the three statuses, Universal, Selective, and Does not apply, by both fill and symbol.'

library(ggplot2)

archs <- c(
  'Data analysis', 'Scholarly manuscript', 'R package',
  'Simulation study', 'Blog'
)
gates <- c(
  'R CMD check', 'Unit tests', 'Render report',
  'Seed determinism'
)
grid <- expand.grid(
  archetype = archs, gate = gates,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

renders <- c('Scholarly manuscript', 'Blog')
seeded <- c('Simulation study')

grid$status <- 'not emphasised'
grid$status[grid$gate %in% c('R CMD check', 'Unit tests')] <-
  'universal'
grid$status[grid$gate == 'Render report' &
              grid$archetype %in% renders] <- 'applies'
grid$status[grid$gate == 'Seed determinism' &
              grid$archetype %in% seeded] <- 'applies'

grid$archetype <- factor(grid$archetype, levels = rev(archs))
grid$gate <- factor(grid$gate, levels = gates)
grid$status <- factor(
  grid$status,
  levels = c('universal', 'applies', 'not emphasised')
)

# Non-color cue: a point shape per status, so universal and
# selective cells differ by shape as well as hue (WCAG 1.4.1).
# The two fills are only 1.34:1 apart, so the shape carries the
# distinction; the white markers are 7.1:1 and 5.3:1 against them.
# Point shapes rather than a text glyph, because the PDF device
# cannot encode a Unicode circle. The shape scale shares the fill
# scale's labels so the two merge into one legend, and a reader who
# cannot separate the hues can still read the key by shape.
marked <- grid[grid$status != 'not emphasised', ]
status_labels <- c(
  'universal'      = 'Universal',
  'applies'        = 'Selective',
  'not emphasised' = 'Does not apply'
)

ggplot(grid, aes(x = gate, y = archetype, fill = status)) +
  geom_tile(colour = 'white', linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = marked, aes(shape = status), colour = 'white',
             size = 3.5) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c('universal' = 16, 'applies' = 17,
               'not emphasised' = NA),
    labels = status_labels, drop = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      'universal'      = '#1a5c8c',
      'applies'        = '#1e7a50',
      'not emphasised' = '#7a8a9c'
    ),
    labels = status_labels
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2.5))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = 'bottom'
  )
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the render-none case

A reviewer objects that a compendium producing no rendered
document cannot be a reproducible research object, since
there is no result to reproduce. Which archetype answers
this objection, and how?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The R-package archetype answers it. A package that exports
a summary-table function has no report to render, yet it is
fully reproducible. Its result is the behavior of the
function, and that behavior is protected by `R CMD check`
and by the unit tests. These regenerate and verify the
function's outputs on every check. The absence of a render
gate does not weaken reproducibility. It reflects only that
the deliverable is a tested procedure rather than a
document.
:::
:::

## How each archetype treats the chapters ahead

The reproducibility machinery is identical across the five
archetypes; only its weight shifts. @tbl-archetype-weight
is the reference every later chapter points back to rather
than restates. For each archetype, it records how the
ladder reads it (@sec-levels) and how heavily it leans on a
[sealed render](glossary.qmd#gloss-sealed-render)
(@sec-literate). It also records which kind of test
carries its weight (@sec-testing) and how its
continuous-integration gates are configured
(@sec-verification). Lastly, it records how much a
pipeline tool earns its keep (@sec-pipelines) and how the
compendium is ultimately shared (@sec-archiving).

| Archetype | Ladder (@sec-levels) | Literate programming (@sec-literate) | Testing (@sec-testing) | CI gates (@sec-verification) | Pipeline (@sec-pipelines) | Sharing (@sec-archiving) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Data analysis | Same rungs as a manuscript; L3 via a baseline on a derived rate | Light; an internal HTML summary, not a typeset report | Leans on data-validation and reproducibility tests | Render gate only if a report exists | Strong case for `targets`, since it is re-run constantly and skipping unchanged steps saves time | Deposited as itself |
| Scholarly manuscript | Full apparatus; L3 compares tables and figures with recorded baselines | Center of gravity; the sealed render this chapter is built around | Adds a report-renders-and-matches-baseline test | Render gate is central, not optional | Modest; often a one-target build around the sealed report | Deposited beside the article it supports |
| R package | L1 and L2 as for any archetype, since `R CMD check` is a gate, not a rung; L3 via a baseline on function output after a clean rebuild | Largely absent; help pages and vignettes stand in | Native home of unit testing; `R CMD check` runs the suite | No render gate unless a vignette exists | None; `R CMD check` plays the corresponding role | Also released to CRAN or an R-universe, not only archived |
| Simulation study | L2 is nominal without the seed discipline; RNG kind is the load-bearing determinant | Thin; a presentation layer over pre-computed, stored results | Leans hardest on the seed-determinism test | A reduced, fixed-seed grid runs under CI; the full grid runs elsewhere | Strongest case of the five; `targets` branching maps the parameter grid | Recorded seeds and the union lockfile are what a re-runner needs |
| Blog | Applies post by post; L3 needs a baseline per post | Central but multiplied across many rendered posts | Tests the code each post's examples depend on | Render gate iterates over every post | Rebuilds only the posts whose sources changed | Deployed as a website; the compendium behind it is still deposited |

: How each archetype treats the topics of the chapters ahead. The reproducibility machinery under every cell is the same; the table records only where the emphasis falls. {#tbl-archetype-weight}

## Progressive disclosure

But must a project choose one archetype and keep it? The
five archetypes can also be stages a single project passes
through. The framework's most useful structural property
is that the same layout supports the whole trajectory
without reorganization. This is what the framework calls
*progressive disclosure*: the same directory layout, the
same `Makefile`, and the same Five Pillars carry a project
from one archetype to the next.

The trajectory is easy to picture, and it is the one our
epidemiology student is likely to walk. The project begins
as a data analysis: scripts and figures, no manuscript. As
the findings firm up, a `report.Rmd` is added to
`analysis/report/` and the project becomes a manuscript
compendium, with the render gate now active. Nothing
already written needs to move. In the course of the
analysis a cleaning routine and a modeling helper prove
useful enough to document and test, so they migrate from
`analysis/scripts/` into `R/`. The package archetype's
gates begin to bite on them without any change to the
layout. Should one of those functions reach general
interest, the compendium can be shared as a package, with
its `R/` and `man/` and `tests/` now first-class. The
`analysis/` directory then recedes to a development
notebook. The same compendium has been, in turn, a data
analysis, a manuscript, and a package, and at no point was
it reorganized.

The archetype therefore describes a project's current
emphasis; it is not a permanent category. The
reproducibility machinery is invariant across the
archetypes and across the transitions between them. It is
this invariance that lets a project evolve without leaving
the reproducible state it started in. The worked example
that follows traces the first part of this trajectory in
detail.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what moves, what does not

In the student's trajectory above, name one thing that
changes at each transition and one thing that never does.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

What changes: the archetype recorded in `zzcollab.yaml`,
and the set of gates that apply (a render gate joins at
the manuscript transition; `R CMD check`'s documentation
and export checks start to bite once functions migrate
into `R/`). What never changes: the directory layout
itself. No file already written is moved or renamed at
either transition, and the Five Pillars sit in the same
three root-level artifacts throughout.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the progressive-disclosure trajectory concrete, we
follow a single compendium through its first two
archetypes. We stay at the level of the directory and the
gates rather than the analysis. Suppose our student begins
the incident-diabetes study. The compendium is created and
its archetype recorded as a data analysis. The shell
session below is illustrative and is not executed.

```bash
$ mkdir diabetes-cohort && cd diabetes-cohort
$ zzc analysis  # tidyverse base-image profile; archetype set separately
```

The student places the registry extract under `raw_data/`
and writes `analysis/scripts/01_clean.R` to produce a
derived cohort table. The student then writes
`analysis/scripts/02_model.R` to fit the Cox model. A unit
test in `inst/tinytest/` asserts the cohort size and that
the fitted hazard ratio matches a value recorded in a
committed baseline file, within a stated tolerance. This
is a test that can actually fail if the model's inputs or
the `survival` version drift. By contrast, a bound such as
'no hazard ratio is negative' would be satisfied by every
correct and every broken fit alike. At this point the only
gates that apply are the universal check and the tests,
run in a clean environment:

```bash
$ make check-renv     # dependencies declared and locked
$ make docker-test    # tinytest only
$ make docker-check   # R CMD check
```

Some weeks later the results are firm enough to write up.
The student adds `analysis/report/report.Rmd`, moving the
figure code out of `02_model.R` and into report chunks that
regenerate the figures on render. The compendium is now a
manuscript, and the archetype line in `zzcollab.yaml` is
updated to reflect it. However, not a single existing file
has moved. A render gate now joins the others:

```bash
$ make docker-render  # rebuild report.Rmd to PDF
```

The cleaning routine, meanwhile, has grown into a general
helper worth documenting. It therefore migrates from
`analysis/scripts/01_clean.R` into `R/prepare_cohort.R`,
gains a `roxygen2` block, and picks up its own unit tests.
The package archetype's discipline now protects it, and
`R CMD check` verifies that the documentation matches the
function signature. The same compendium is now doing the
work of three archetypes at once, on one unchanged layout.
Each gate applies to the part of the project that warrants
it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the manuscript transition

When `report.Rmd` is added and the project becomes a
manuscript compendium, what single gate becomes active
that was not before, and what about the compendium's
Five Pillars status is unaffected by this transition?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The render gate becomes active: a validation run must now
rebuild `report.Rmd` to PDF, where before there was no
report to render. The Five Pillars are unaffected, because
adding a manuscript changes which gates apply, not which
artifacts capture the environment, the packages, the
session, the code, or the data. Those five pillars are the
same five files or records before and after the archetype
changes.
:::
:::

## The cohort, continued

The examples so far have all described a hypothetical
student's compendium. We now perform the same
classification exercise on this book's own running cohort
compendium, as it sits in this repository when the
chapter is rendered.

```{r}
raw <- load_cohort('../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
pillars <- c(
  environment_dockerfile = file.exists('../../Dockerfile'),
  packages_renv_lock = file.exists('../../renv.lock'),
  session_rprofile = file.exists('../../.Rprofile'),
  source_code_r_cohort = file.exists('../../R/cohort.R'),
  data_generator = file.exists('../scripts/simulate_cohort.R')
)
pillars
sum(pillars)
nrow(raw)
nrow(cohort)
pillar_label <- c(
  environment_dockerfile = 'the environment pillar (`Dockerfile`)',
  packages_renv_lock = 'the package-versions pillar (`renv.lock`)',
  session_rprofile = 'the session pillar (`.Rprofile`)',
  source_code_r_cohort = 'the source-code pillar (`R/cohort.R`)',
  data_generator = 'the data pillar (`simulate_cohort.R`)'
)
pillars_absent <- if (any(!pillars)) {
  paste(pillar_label[!pillars], collapse = ' and ')
} else {
  'no pillar'
}
rung <- if (pillars[['packages_renv_lock']] &&
              pillars[['environment_dockerfile']]) {
  'L2'
} else if (pillars[['packages_renv_lock']]) {
  'L1'
} else {
  'L0'
}
```

In this repository, `r sum(pillars)` of the Five Pillars
have an artifact. The source-code pillar is `R/cohort.R`,
under version control. The data pillar is the committed
generator `analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R`, which
writes the synthetic extract from a fixed seed; the CSV it
writes is gitignored, so the chunk checks the generator,
not the extract. Of the five, the compendium still lacks
`r pillars_absent`. Against the archetype table above,
this compendium is a **data analysis**. Its deliverable is
the pipeline of `R/cohort.R` and the chunks this book's
chapters run against it, not a rendered manuscript of its
own. The applicable gates are therefore the universal
`R CMD check` and the unit tests, with no render gate
required. Measured against the Five Pillars, the
compendium is at **`r rung`**, the rung @sec-levels
computes for it from the same files. The lockfile entry,
`r pillars[['packages_renv_lock']]`, and the Dockerfile
entry, `r pillars[['environment_dockerfile']]`, decide the
rung. The source-code and data pillars make a compendium
locatable, and the session pillar fixes the options a
session starts with, but none of the three pins a package
version or an environment.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: pillars present, rung reached

This compendium currently has `r sum(pillars)` of the Five
Pillars captured by an artifact, with `r pillars_absent`
absent. Does holding `r sum(pillars)` of five pillars,
`r round(100 * sum(pillars) / 5)` percent of them, place it
partway between two rungs of the ladder of @sec-levels?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The ladder is not a count of pillars. It is a
cumulative scale in which L1 specifically requires the
package-versions pillar (`renv.lock`) and L2 specifically
requires the environment pillar (`Dockerfile`) as well.
With the lockfile entry `r pillars[['packages_renv_lock']]`
and the Dockerfile entry
`r pillars[['environment_dockerfile']]`, the compendium is
at `r rung`, and the other pillars present add nothing to
that placement. Four of five pillars with the lockfile
present and the Dockerfile absent is L1, not 80 percent of
the way to L2. No rung is reached by partial credit across
unrelated pillars.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for scaffolding and
organizing a compendium. However, it is an unreliable one
for the judgments that define it. The three triples below
mark the division.

{{< include _llm-rule.qmd >}}

A compendium's own directory listing can be enough to
tempt a reader into pasting what it names. The prompts
below describe the structure instead, with file names
rather than file contents.

**Prompt.** 'I have a folder of R scripts and CSV files for
a cohort analysis. Propose a research-compendium directory
structure and tell me which files go where.'

*Watch for.* A plausible layout that silently guesses the
raw-and-derived boundary, placing a file the model cannot
distinguish as input or output into the wrong directory.
Watch also for an omission of the R-package skin
(`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`) that quietly forfeits the
`R CMD check` gate.

*Verification.* Confirm by hand that every file in
`raw_data/` is a genuine immutable input and every file in
`derived_data/` is regenerable from code, because this is
the analyst's judgment and not the model's. Confirm the
R-package skin is present, and run `R CMD check` to
establish that the proposed structure is in fact checkable,
remembering that the check covers `R/` and the tests, not
the scripts under `analysis/`.

*A better prompt.* 'Below is a list of the file names in
my cohort analysis, with no contents, and a note of which
files the data office sent me. Propose a compendium layout
with an R-package skin (`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, `R/`,
`analysis/`). For each file, say raw or derived and why;
mark any file you cannot classify rather than guessing.
Then list the commands I should run to check the layout.'

**Prompt.** 'Which archetype should this project be, and
which validation gates apply?'

*Watch for.* Check whether the answer defaults to the
manuscript archetype when the project has no report and is
really a package or a simulation study. Check also whether
it lists, with confidence, a render gate for a project
that renders nothing.

*Verification.* Decide the archetype yourself from the
project's actual deliverable, a document, a function, or a
set of stored simulation results, and then check that the
gates the model lists match @tbl-archetypes for that
archetype. A render gate on a render-none package is the
tell that the model has guessed the archetype wrongly.

**Prompt.** 'Write the unit tests that should gate this
compendium.'

*Watch for.* Tests that assert only that functions exist or
that a script runs without error, which are structural
checks rather than correctness tests. For a simulation
compendium, watch also for an absence of any test that the
seeded output is reproducible.

*Verification.* Read each generated test and confirm it
checks a value the analysis actually depends on, not merely
that code executes. For a simulation study, add or verify a
test that compares the seeded output with a baseline
recorded in an earlier session and committed, within a
stated tolerance (@sec-testing). That is the property the
archetype exists to protect, so check for it first. A
second call in the same
session agrees with the first even when the generator has
changed, so it does not test this. If an agent writes the
tests, it can also run them and edit them until they pass.
The expected values and the recorded baseline stay with
the analyst, who reads every change under `inst/tinytest/`
and `inst/baseline/` before it is merged
(@sec-llm-delegate).

## Exercises

1. Take an existing analysis of your own, currently a
   scatter of scripts and data files, and classify it as
   one of the five archetypes. State the deliverable that
   determines the classification, and list the validation
   gates that should apply on top of `R CMD check`.

2. For that same analysis, draw the raw-and-derived
   boundary explicitly: list every data file and assign it
   to `raw_data/` or `derived_data/`, justifying each
   assignment by whether the file is an immutable input or a
   regenerable product. Identify any file whose status is
   genuinely ambiguous and explain the ambiguity.

3. Explain, in a paragraph, why `R CMD check` is described
   in this chapter as a universal gate. What does dressing a
   compendium in the R-package skin buy that a plain,
   well-named folder does not?

4. Sketch a progressive-disclosure trajectory for a project
   that begins as a simulation study and ends as an R
   package. At each transition, state which gate becomes
   active or inactive, and confirm that no directory needs
   to be reorganized.

5. Consider a simulation compendium whose driver script
   contains no `set.seed()` call. At which rung of the
   reproducibility ladder can such a compendium sit at best,
   and why can it not, even in principle, reach L3? Write
   the one-line test you would add to gate the seeding.

6. The chapter claims that the manuscript is only one of
   five archetypes. Construct the strongest argument you can
   for the opposing view, that every serious research
   compendium should ultimately produce a rendered document,
   and then state where the argument fails.

7. On this book's own running cohort compendium, run
   `load_cohort()` and `clean_cohort()` from `R/cohort.R`
   against `analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv`, as in
   'The cohort, continued' above, and separately check
   `file.exists()` for the five artifacts the `pillars` chunk
   checks: `Dockerfile`, `renv.lock`, and `.Rprofile` at the
   project root, `R/cohort.R`, and the generator
   `analysis/scripts/simulate_cohort.R`. Report three numbers
   a grading script could check without fitting any model:
   the raw row count, the cleaned row count, and how many of
   the Five Pillars have an artifact present when you run
   the check.

8. This exercise returns to the reproducibility ladder of
   Chapter 3 (@sec-levels). Using the pillar count and the
   `file.exists()` results from Exercise 7, state which
   single rung of the L0-L3 ladder this book's own cohort
   compendium occupies when you run the check, and explain
   why the number of pillars captured does not place it
   partway between two rungs.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. The first
two work on an analysis of your own, so what you produce
will vary; the boxes say what a good answer establishes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
that the classification follows from the **deliverable**,
not from the subject matter or the size of the project.

The discriminating question is what the project is *for*.
If the answer is a paper, it is a scholarly manuscript and
the render gate applies. If it is a set of results with no
document, it is a data analysis and the render gate may or
may not apply. If it is a function other people will call,
it is an R package and the render gate does not apply at
all. If it is an estimate of an operating characteristic
obtained by repeated sampling, it is a simulation study and
the seed-determinism gate applies. If it is a post, it is a
blog.

The gates on top of the universal `R CMD check` are drawn
from a short list. Unit tests apply universally; the render
gate applies where a document is the deliverable; and seed
determinism applies where the result is stochastic. Naming
a gate that does not apply is as much the point of the
exercise as naming one that does, since the chapter's
claim is that the machinery is identical and only the
gates differ.

If you find that your analysis is genuinely two
archetypes, a manuscript that also ships a reusable
function, you have found the ordinary case rather than an
anomaly, and you should apply the union of the gates.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
the operative test, which is not 'is this file original'
but **'if I deleted this file, could the code regenerate
it?'**

If yes, it is derived. If no, it is raw, and it needs a
provenance record and a checksum, because nothing in the
compendium can reconstruct it.

Two ambiguous cases arise often enough to expect them. The
first is a **cleaned extract received from a data
coordinating center**. It is derived from someone's raw
data, but not from anything in this compendium, so it is
raw here: the compendium's code cannot regenerate it. The
rule is that the boundary is drawn at the edge of *this*
compendium, not at the edge of the world. The second is a **manually
corrected file**, where an analyst fixed a handful of
values by hand. It is not regenerable, because the
corrections live nowhere but in the file, so it must be
treated as raw. The better resolution is to make it derived
by recording the corrections as code, a lookup table of
overrides applied by a script, which restores
regenerability and makes the corrections reviewable.

A third case worth naming is a **cached expensive
computation**, a model that took a day to fit. It is
derived by the test, since the code can regenerate it, but
storing it is sensible. It belongs in `derived_data/` and
should be regenerable on demand rather than trusted
indefinitely.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

`R CMD check` is universal because it is the one gate that
applies to every archetype regardless of deliverable. A
manuscript, a simulation, a blog, and a package all carry
the same skin. That is, each has functions in `R/` that
must load, declared dependencies that must resolve, and
tests that must pass. `R CMD check` verifies exactly those
three things without knowing or caring what the project
produces. The
archetype-specific gates, rendering a document and
checking seed determinism, apply to some archetypes and
not others; this one applies to all of them.

A complete answer also states the limit. The check runs on
the built package, and `.Rbuildignore` excludes
`analysis/`, so it never parses or runs the analysis
scripts. A script there can carry a syntax error or an
undeclared package and the check still passes. 'Universal'
means it applies to every archetype, not that it covers
every file. The analysis code is gated by the render gate
and the dependency scan of @sec-verification.

What the R-package skin buys over a well-named folder is
**an existing verification apparatus that the project
becomes eligible for**. A plain folder can hold all five
artifacts and can in principle reach any rung of the
ladder, so the skin buys nothing in terms of capture. What
it buys is that `DESCRIPTION` and `NAMESPACE` are the
interface `R CMD check` expects. Supplying that interface
makes a large, mature, externally maintained body of checks
apply to the analysis for free. Without it there is no
single standard command that verifies the code loads and
the dependencies resolve. The analyst must then assemble
an equivalent by hand, differently, for every project.

This is the same bargain as any other standard format: the
structure is arbitrary in itself and useful because other
things already understand it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

A serviceable trajectory has three transitions.

**Simulation study.** The seed-determinism gate is active,
since the results are draws and their reproducibility
depends on the generator. `R CMD check` and unit tests are
active, as always. The render gate is inactive: there is no
document yet.

**Simulation study plus a report on its findings.** The
render gate becomes active. Seeding stays active, since the
simulation still runs. Nothing else changes.

**R package, the simulation logic extracted into exported
functions.** The render gate becomes inactive again if the
report is dropped, or stays active if a vignette replaces
it, which is the usual outcome. Seed determinism becomes
inactive as a *project* gate and reappears inside the unit
tests, as an assertion that a seeded function returns a
recorded value. `R CMD check` becomes more demanding rather
